strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: enabling training-free, reference-based motion customization on few-step distilled video generators (T2V-Turbo-V2, AnimateDiff-Lightning), where existing training-free methods fail due to the coarse sampling schedule and mismatched denoising behavior. The problem analysis (Sec. 1, Fig. 2) is informative and well-motivated.

The proposed teacher-guided test-time distillation with endpoint prediction and interpolation is a sensible solution: running motion customization on a fine-grained teacher and injecting guidance into the student via distillation loss preserves motion fidelity while keeping the student few-step. The adaptive acceleration strategy (step-wise guidance activation with moving-average loss and dynamic truncation) is a reasonable engineering contribution to balance cost and quality.

Experimental evidence is relatively thorough for this type of work: two different student/teacher model families, two benchmarks (TurboBench with 66 pairs, AnimateBench with 15 videos), multiple metrics (temporal consistency, text alignment, motion fidelity, FID, inference/training time), a 50-participant user study, component-wise ablations (Tab. 3) that clearly show each piece's contribution, and supplementary hyperparameter ablations (λ, η, k) plus pseudo-code in Algorithm 1, which supports reproducibility.

Strong efficiency results: ~13s at 16 steps and competitive quality at 8 or 4 steps, substantially faster than training-free baselines like MotionClone (114s) or DMT (316s), with better motion fidelity — a meaningful practical win rather than a marginal one. Limitations and ethical impacts are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: the framework is essentially MotionClone-style temporal-attention guidance applied to a full teacher model, run in parallel with the student, plus linear interpolation of the two one-step predictions and two threshold-based heuristics. There is limited theoretical or empirical justification for why the interpolation (Eq. 5) is the right way to inject teacher guidance, and no analysis of failure modes of the distillation loss itself.

The method is heavily hand-tuned and model-specific: thresholds δ1, δ2, window size W, τ, λ, η, k are all determined by grid search and differ between backbones (δ1 ranges 380–420 for TurboV2 vs. 360–400 for AD-L, given in raw loss units). This raises concerns about robustness and generalization to new models, which the paper acknowledges only implicitly.

Evaluation concerns: benchmarks are small (66 text-video pairs, 15 reference videos), and the FID computation against a tiny self-constructed reference set yields implausibly large values (320–380), making its absolute value and discriminative power questionable. Baselines are compared on their native (slow) models rather than being given an equal teacher-compute budget, and the user study (36 samples, win rates ~42–53%) shows sizable non-ours preference mass that is not analyzed statistically.

Writing and presentation need polish: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('algin', 'according motion types', 'training-free methods injecting motion priors', 'the customized teacher provide guidance by refine', 'Aaptive acceleration', 'T2V-Trubo-V2', 'ContolVideo'), inconsistent figure labeling (MC vs. MotionClone), and a broken/incomplete project-page link. Equation notation (e.g., z_t^θ trajectory initialization) requires careful decoding despite Algorithm 1 helping.

The efficiency claim should be qualified: the teacher branch performs up to Nmax inner denoising steps per student step, so worst-case cost can approach full-teacher inference (ablation shows 20s vs. 13s with adaptive acceleration); the paper does not report the distribution of activated teacher steps or sensitivity to δ1/δ2, making the adaptive strategy's behavior hard to assess. No code is released yet (promised only), limiting immediate reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and timely problem: existing training-free motion customization methods (MotionClone, DMT) degrade significantly when applied to few-step distilled video generators, and the authors clearly motivate why (collapsed denoising steps, behavioral mismatch with the teacher, ineffectiveness of inversion-based approaches).

The core idea of test-time distillation—using a slow, motion-customized teacher to correct the student's one-step predictions via endpoint prediction and interpolation—is a sensible and reasonably novel combination of score distillation and inference-time guidance.

The adaptive acceleration strategy (step-wise guidance activation via a moving-average motion loss and dynamic truncation of the teacher loop) is a practical contribution that partially mitigates the extra cost of teacher guidance.

Experiments cover two student/teacher families (T2V-Turbo-V2/VideoCrafter2 and AnimateDiff-Lightning/AnimateDiff), with quantitative comparisons against both training-based and training-free baselines, ablation studies of each component, hyperparameter ablations (λ, η, k), and a user study; pseudo-code in the supplementary improves reproducibility.
The limitations and societal-impact discussions are present and substantive.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the framework is essentially MotionClone's temporal-attention guidance (reused nearly verbatim as Eq. 3 and the motion loss) plus a straightforward interpolation with a teacher's prediction, reminiscent of existing distillation-guided sampling. The adaptive acceleration components are simple heuristic thresholds rather than a principled mechanism.

The method is heavily hyperparameter-dependent and brittle: the activation threshold δ1 must be set per motion type (380–420 for TurboV2, 360–400 for AD-L), plus δ2, window size W, max teacher steps Nmax, blend factor k, and guidance strengths, all determined by grid search on the evaluation data. This undermines the 'training-free, plug-and-play' narrative and raises concerns about generalization to unseen motion types.

The efficiency claim is weaker than presented: the method requires running a full-size teacher model with iterative denoising and motion-gradient backpropagation whenever guidance activates. The 13s vs. MotionClone's 114s comparison is favorable, but the ablation shows the teacher-guided variant costs 20s versus 4–7s for pure student inference; the true wall-clock and memory cost relative to the advertised 'fast' distilled models is not fully transparent.

Evaluation scale is small and non-standard: TurboBench has only 66 video-edit pairs from 22 videos, and AnimateBench only 15 videos. FID is computed against a reference set built from the same small source videos, making the FID gains (e.g., 322.97 vs. 351–383) statistically fragile. The user study covers 36 samples and 50 participants.

Baseline fairness concerns: training-free baselines (DMT, MotionClone) run on the slow teacher model with dense steps, while the proposed method benefits from a distilled student plus a teacher; some baselines' settings (steps, guidance configurations) are not fully matched, and MotionDirector/MotionInversion are training-based methods evaluated under different conditions.

Only one ablation configuration is reported (TurboV2 on TurboBench); the AnimateDiff family is covered only by final comparisons. Notable internal inconsistencies (e.g., in Table 2, MC+AD-L reports motion fidelity 0.648 at 7s while MotionClone reports 0.849 at 203s) are not explained and weaken confidence in the tables.

Scope is limited to U-Net-based VideoCrafter/AnimateDiff lineages where the student and teacher share architecture; applicability to modern DiT-based distilled generators (HunyuanVideo, Wan, CogVideoX) — the models users actually deploy — is neither demonstrated nor discussed.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: the project page link is empty, there are numerous typos and grammatical errors ('algin', 'T2V-Trubo-V2', 'Aaptive acceleration strategy', 'the customized teacher provide guidance by refine'), and the transition around Eq. 5 (score distillation loss vs. simple linear interpolation z_new = (1−λ)ẑψ + λẑθ) is confusingly written.

The claim that the method 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-based and training-free approaches' overstates the evidence given the small benchmarks, metric fragility, and narrow model coverage.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: enabling training-free motion customization on distilled (few-step) video generators, where existing training-free methods (MotionClone, DMT) demonstrably fail. The motivating analysis of why distilled models break progressive guidance is insightful.

The proposed test-time distillation framework is well motivated: using a fine-grained teacher with motion customization to guide the student via endpoint prediction interpolation is a sensible and technically coherent solution, and the adaptive acceleration strategy (step-wise guidance activation via moving-window motion loss and dynamic truncation) is a thoughtful addition for the efficiency-quality trade-off.

Experimental evidence is reasonably comprehensive: two distinct student/teacher model families (T2V-Turbo-V2/VideoCrafter2 and AnimateDiff-Lightning/AnimateDiff), quantitative comparison against six baselines across five metrics, an ablation study isolating each component (Tab. 3), supplementary ablations over all key hyperparameters, and a 50-participant user study supporting the automatic metrics.

The efficiency results are convincing: the method outperforms training-free baselines on motion fidelity, text alignment, and FID while running in 13s (16 steps) vs. 114s (MotionClone) and 316s (DMT), and remains competitive at 8 and 4 steps.

The paper is generally well organized, with pseudocode in the supplementary material aiding reproducibility, and includes a meaningful limitations discussion and a substantive ethical/societal impact section.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the framework is largely a careful combination of known ingredients — MotionClone-style temporal-attention energy guidance, DDIM-inverted noise blending (FreeTraj/FreeNoise), and teacher-student score distillation via prediction interpolation. No new theoretical insight or fundamentally new algorithmic mechanism is introduced; the contribution is primarily applied/engineering in nature.

The efficiency claim needs qualification. The method is 'training-free' but requires running the slow teacher model (with iterative inner denoising, up to Nmax steps per student step) during inference; the 13s runtime is nearly 4x slower than simply applying MotionClone to the distilled model (7s) and far slower than the plain distilled model. The claim of 'maintaining high efficiency' holds relative to slow baselines, but the framing underplays this dependence on an expensive teacher at test time.

Heavy reliance on manually tuned, per-model hyperparameters: thresholds δ1 and δ2 differ across backbones (380-420/380 for TurboV2; 360-400/360 for AD-L), plus τ, λ, η, k, W, Nmax determined by grid search. This raises concerns about generalization to new model pairs and weakens the plug-and-play character implied by 'training-free'. Sensitivity analysis for δ1, δ2, τ, Nmax is missing from the supplementary ablations.

Benchmarks are small and custom: TurboBench has only 66 video-edit pairs from 22 videos, and AnimateBench only 15 reference videos. Given this scale, differences of ~0.01-0.02 in CLIP-based metrics (e.g., text alignment 0.348 vs. 0.335) may not be statistically meaningful; no variance/significance reporting is provided.

The reported FID values (320-380 for all methods, where lower-res distilled variants score 'better') are difficult to interpret, and the reference image set construction from 'selected source videos' is under-specified; the metric choice deserves more justification.

Temporal consistency of the full method (0.976) is essentially at parity with MotionClone (0.978) and below the unguided distilled model (0.973→0.973 in ablation), so motion quality gains partly trade against text alignment/temporal stability in some configurations; this trade-off could be discussed more candidly.

The approach is restricted to student models that have a matching strong teacher with the same architecture (VC2/TurboV2, AD/AD-L), limiting applicability to modern architecture-mismatched pairs; the paper acknowledges restricted model scope only briefly.

Minor issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('algin', 'we make a a thorough analysis', 'provide guidance by refine', 'Aaptive', figure labels 'ContolVideo', 'snowy filed'), code availability only promised, and the project page link is blank.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: the paper provides both empirical (Fig. 2, Table 3) and analytical evidence for why existing training-free motion customization methods fail on distilled video generators, which is a novel and practically relevant observation.

The proposed MotionEcho framework is technically sound: teacher re-noising of the student's anchor, closed-form score interpolation (Eq. 5), and a detailed derivation of the equivalent proximal and noise-prediction forms (Appendix C) make the method easy to understand and verify.

The adaptive acceleration strategy (step-wise guidance activation + dynamic truncation) is a sensible mechanism to balance quality and cost, and is ablated convincingly (Table 3: MF 0.833 → 0.912 → 0.933 while ITC drops from 20s to 13s).

Very broad experimental coverage: the method is validated on multiple distilled backbones (T2V-Turbo-V2, Video-Blade, AnimateDiff-Lightning, TDM, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Fastvideo/Turbo) with multiple motion guidance variants (MotionClone, MOFT, DMT, DiTFlow), including extra benchmarks (LOVEU-TGVE) and metrics (Flow-sim), demonstrating architecture-agnostic generalization.

Comprehensive supplementary material with pseudo-code, hyperparameter ablations (λ, η, δ1, δ2), memory/runtime analysis, a failure case, and an ethics discussion; the limitations section is honest and specific.
Large efficiency gains over existing alternatives (e.g., 35x–402x speedups reported in Fig. 1) and strong user-study win rates.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading in spirit: the method requires loading and running a full, heavyweight teacher diffusion model (VideoCrafter2 or Wan2.1/Wan2.2) at inference time, doubling peak memory (36 GB on TurboV2, Table 12) and roughly doubling inference time over the distilled backbone. The efficiency advantage over baselines depends on this extra teacher resource, which could be discussed more prominently in the main text.

Gains on some metrics are marginal: text alignment improvements over MotionClone are small (0.348 vs 0.335), and temporal consistency occasionally decreases with motion guidance (Table 3, 0.973 → 0.967), while the main wins are in motion fidelity — the paper's claims are mostly accurate but headline improvements are narrower than they first appear.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and tuning burden: several hyperparameters are hand-set per motion type (η, k, δ1, δ2 differ for camera/object/hybrid motion in the appendix), which weakens the plug-and-play 'seamlessly integrated' claim and complicates reproducibility; code is only promised upon acceptance.

The evaluation relies partly on image-level FID for videos with unusually large absolute values (320–380), and metric definitions (e.g., MF based on Co-Tracker geometric consistency) are borrowed rather than validated; per-frame CLIP-based TA/TC may not capture fine-grained motion quality, though the added optical-flow metric and user study partially mitigate this.

Core components are largely compositions of existing techniques (MotionClone-style motion energy guidance, SDS-like distillation objectives, learned-scheduler heuristics); novelty rests mainly on the trajectory-restoration idea and its adaptation to few-step sampling, which is valuable but incremental in its individual parts.

Comparisons between distilled-student outputs and full-model baselines on the same benchmarks are not compute-matched in all tables (e.g., MotionClone 114s vs. Ours 13s), which is favorable to the paper; a compute-matched comparison at the teacher's budget would strengthen the efficiency claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely relevant and under-explored problem: why existing training-free motion customization methods fail on distilled (few-step) video generators, and how to restore motion control without giving up fast sampling. The motivation and failure analysis (Sec. 3.2) is a useful contribution in itself.

The proposed framework is clearly described: teacher-guided trajectory correction via re-noising the student's endpoint onto the teacher's dense trajectory, an SDS-style objective that reduces to a closed-form linear interpolation (Eq. 5, with a proximal interpretation in the appendix), and an adaptive acceleration strategy with step-wise activation and dynamic truncation.

Experiments are unusually broad for this area: five distinct distilled backbones (T2V-Turbo-V2, Video-Blade, AnimateDiff-Lightning, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-FastVideo/Turbo, TDM on CogVideoX-2B), two custom benchmarks plus LOVEU-TGVE, quantitative comparisons with training-based and training-free baselines, user study (50 participants), hyperparameter ablations, per-motion-type stratified metrics including an optical-flow-based metric, and a memory/time analysis.

The ablation study (Table 3) cleanly disentangles motion guidance, teacher guidance, and adaptive acceleration, showing each component contributes (MF: 0.562 -> 0.833 -> 0.912 -> 0.933) and that the adaptive strategy recovers much of the teacher-guidance cost.
The supplementary material is thorough: pseudo-code, derivations, extensive qualitative results across motion types, an honest failure case, limitations discussion, and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: The core efficiency claim is weaker than advertised. The method requires the full, undistilled teacher model at inference time: ITC rises from 4s to 13s on TurboV2 and 33s to ~50s on VB, and peak memory from 27GB to 36GB. This substantially erodes the practical value of distillation for deployment (the whole point of a distilled student is to avoid the teacher), and the paper is 'training-free' only in the fine-tuning sense. The necessity of a paired teacher with a shared latent space is acknowledged as a limitation but is a significant practical restriction.

Novelty is moderate: the approach is essentially MotionClone/DMT/DiTFlow-style test-time guidance applied inside a teacher loop, combined with a simple linear interpolation to the teacher target. The 'closed-form' update is a one-line linear blend; the adaptive scheduling adds two hand-tuned thresholds (delta_1, delta_2), with per-motion-type values in the appendix ((500,500), (500,460), (480,380)), raising concerns about tuning sensitivity and generality.

Not all results support the headline claims. On DavisBench (Table 2), text alignment drops relative to all baselines (0.311-0.313 vs 0.321-0.326) and FID is comparable or slightly worse than DMT (130-132.5 vs 129.49). In Table 9, MotionClone's camera-motion MF (0.940) actually marginally exceeds ours (0.938), yet the text claims outperformance on both subsets. The wins concentrate on MF, and MF gains over weak distilled baselines are less meaningful.

Evaluation metrics and benchmarks are partly self-defined. 'TurboBench' (66 pairs) and 'DavisBench' (34 videos) are small custom sets; FID values (~320-350) computed on such tiny reference sets are of limited reliability and hard to compare with the literature. Standard motion-customization benchmarks or third-party human evaluation protocols would strengthen the evidence.

The claim that 'distillation fundamentally alters the denoising dynamics' is supported only empirically (Fig. 2 and qualitative observations); no quantitative or formal analysis of trajectory mismatch is provided, so the diagnosis remains somewhat anecdotal.

Several citations appear erroneous or implausible (e.g., references dated 2026, an arXiv ID '2601.15968', CVPR proceedings page numbers for 2026), which raises concerns about reference accuracy and care in preparation.

The efficiency comparison in Fig. 1 (12.67x-402x speedups) is somewhat misleading, as the baselines are slow training-based/training-free methods on full models; the fairer comparison is against the distilled student itself, where the overhead is ~2-3x inference time and up to +9GB memory.

strengths: Identifies an important and timely gap: existing training-free motion customization methods fail on distilled/few-step video generators. The diagnostic experiments (Fig. 2, Table 3 baseline rows) and the analysis of why distillation breaks guidance (large-step dynamics, loss of dense intermediate states) motivate the approach well.

The proposed test-time teacher-guided trajectory correction is a sensible and well-motivated design: renoising the student's predicted endpoint onto the teacher's dense trajectory, then a closed-form interpolation that bypasses the network Jacobian. The derivation in Appendix C (proximal/SDS interpretation) is clean and adds clarity.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: comparisons against both training-based and training-free baselines on multiple backbones (T2V-Turbo-V2, Video-Blade, AnimateDiff-Lightning, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, TDM/CogVideoX), two/three benchmarks, a user study (50 participants, 4 dimensions), and detailed ablations of each component (MG, TG, AA) plus hyperparameter sensitivity (λ, η, δ1, δ2).
Practical efficiency story is quantified honestly (Tables 12, memory/time analysis), and the adaptive acceleration strategy demonstrably reduces ITC from 20s to 13s with no quality loss.

Good completeness and transparency: pseudocode, implementation details, per-type motion metrics (Table 9), a third-party benchmark (LOVEU-TGVE), a failure case with analysis, and explicit limitations and societal-impact sections. Paper is clearly written overall.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is moderate: the method combines an existing guidance loss (MotionClone/DiTFlow/etc.) with a fairly simple interpolation toward a teacher-corrected endpoint. The 'SDS objective' reduces to a linear interpolation, so the theoretical framing (Eq. 5, Appendix C) is more elaborate than the underlying operation. Originality rests mainly on problem framing and system design rather than new guidance mathematics.

Efficiency claims need qualification: although faster than full teacher inference and training-based methods, the framework requires the full teacher model at inference time, roughly doubling peak memory (36 GB on TurboV2; ~+2 GB on VB). The teacher runs multiple inner denoising iterations per activated step, so the 'distilled efficiency' advantage is partially traded away; this trade-off could be foregrounded more prominently.

Hyperparameters appear somewhat hand-tuned and motion-type specific (e.g., separate (δ1, δ2) settings for camera/hybrid/object motion, per-type noise blend factors k). This weakens the claim that the method is a plug-and-play, robustly deployable solution, and could complicate adoption on new motion types.

Evaluation benchmarks are small and partly self-constructed (TurboBench: 66 pairs from 22 videos; DavisBench: 34 videos), with reference sets built by the authors for FID; results could be sensitive to this curation. The LOVEU-TGVE evaluation helps but omits some strongest recent training-free baselines on that benchmark.

Some comparisons have fairness/interpretability caveats: baselines operate on different backbones (e.g., Table 1 compares VC2-based methods against TurboV2-based ours at different step counts), MotionDirector* is a reproduction, and the reported FID values (~320-380) are absolute-quality proxies for which cross-backbone interpretation is delicate. The adaptive acceleration introduces stochasticity (re-noising with fresh noise) that is not analyzed for variance across seeds.

Minor clarity issues: the text occasionally oversells ('fundamentally intractable' Jacobian claims, 'severe dynamic mismatch' argued mostly qualitatively); a quantitative characterization of the distilled-vs-teacher dynamics mismatch (e.g., guidance gradient norms across timesteps) would strengthen the analysis section.
